query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a targeted trace addition of a ductilizing element that preferentially segregates to the lamellar phase boundaries, combined with a controlled annealing treatment to promote its segregation, will improve room-temperature tensile ductility by facilitating smoother dislocation transmission across internal interfaces while retaining or slightly increasing the alloy's strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colony microstructure that exhibits limited room-temperature tensile ductility due to dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
generation.intervention: Add a small concentration of a ductilizing element (e.g., Cu) that is expected to segregate to the phase boundaries, followed by an optimized annealing treatment to enhance the segregation.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing (e.g., strain rate around 10^(-3) s^(-1)), with standard laboratory environmental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemically modified phase boundaries (lamellar interfaces) where the dopant segregates.
generation.mechanism: The dopant segregation reduces the barrier for dislocation motion at the internal boundaries, thereby alleviating local stress concentrations from dislocation pile-ups. This promotes smoother dislocation transmission across the lamellar interfaces, decreasing microcrack formation and catastrophic damage during straining.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to display increased tensile ductility (higher elongation to failure) while maintaining or slightly increasing the yield and ultimate tensile strength compared to the untreated state.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy shows brittleness and limited tensile ductility due to significant dislocation accumulation at internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is bounded by achieving sufficient and uniform dopant segregation; non-optimal dopant concentration or annealing conditions may not overcome the inherent dislocation pile-up issue.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in ductility and the optimal dopant concentration and annealing parameters remain uncertain until experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the eutectic high-entropy alloy: one batch with the trace addition of the ductilizing element (with the subsequent annealing treatment) and one control batch without any dopant addition. Conduct microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM with EDS mapping) to assess the degree of dopant segregation at the phase boundaries, followed by room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure from tensile tests.
Microstructural characterization (TEM, EDS) to verify dopant segregation and dislocation distribution.
Fractographic analysis to examine crack initiation and propagation patterns.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped and annealed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in dislocation pile-ups at the lamellar interfaces and fail to exhibit an improvement in tensile ductility (or display reduced strength), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5). chosen.why: This move most directly addresses the unexplained behavior of dislocation pile-ups by altering the internal boundary chemistry. By promoting ductile boundary behavior through controlled solute segregation, the intervention aims to reduce local stress concentrations and microcracking while maintaining or even improving strength. The approach is well aligned with standard composition-change methods in materials science, making it a plausible single‐intervention study from a research group.

decision.trend: Early studies on eutectic high-entropy alloys focused on designing a dual-phase lamellar microstructure to combine high strength with acceptable ductility. Initially, the as‐cast eutectic alloy–with its alternating soft and hard phases–showed promise but suffered from issues like dislocation pile‐up at phase boundaries. Subsequent work then employed severe thermomechanical treatments (e.g., cryo‐rolling and annealing, hybrid-rolling, and phase‐selective recrystallization) to modify the inherited lamellar architecture, refine microstructures, and better distribute strain. These approaches improved the overall ductility and work hardening, yet the underlying problem of dislocation accumulation at the internal boundaries remained only partly addressed by the processing routes.
decision.unsolved: Despite achieving enhanced strength-ductility synergy through microstructural refinement and heterogeneity, a critical unresolved issue is the inherent tendency of dislocations to pile up at the internal lamellar boundaries. This leads to local stress concentrations, microcracking, and eventual catastrophic failure during room-temperature tensile loading.
decision.lever: grain boundary segregation of ductilizing elements via targeted trace additions (e.g., a carefully chosen dopant that preferentially segregates to phase boundaries) combined with a dedicated annealing treatment to enhance segregation
decision.why: Modifying the boundary chemistry directly addresses the root cause of dislocation pile-up by promoting more efficient dislocation transmission across the lamellar interfaces and reducing stress concentrations. This single intervention occupies the niche of explaining the unexplained boundary behavior, is supported by trends in earlier work that emphasized interface refinement through processing, and is precisely tailored to overcome the brittleness observed in the untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy.
